newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis reaches three-month mark.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis reaches three-month mark.

text.p: The Lima hostage crisis reached its three-month mark on Monday -- still a propaganda dream for the Tupac Amaru rebels, but a gruelling trial for their 72 captives and a nightmare for the Peruvian government.
Families of the hostages holed up in the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence planned a day of solidarity including a nationwide demonstration at midday (1700 GMT).
At that time, hundreds of churches are due to chime bells, while motorists have been urged to sound horns and others to whistle or bang pots and pans in the streets.

"All Peruvians, when the clocks strike midday, should sound any object as a show of solidarity with our families who have been deprived of their liberty for three months," said one relative, who asked not to be named.
An open letter from the families described the time since the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) takeover of the diplomatic compound as "three months of agony and suffering."

More than 500 hostages were initially taken on Dec. 17 when some 20 jungle-trained rebels blew a hole in the residence's outer wall, swarmed into the building during a fierce shootout, and won control in minutes.
The MRTA gradually released most of its prisoners, however, keeping those it considered most valuable as bargaining chips in its central aim of freeing some 400 jailed comrades.

The remaining captives -- a glittering list of top diplomats, security chiefs, ministers, judges and businessmen - - are mainly middle-aged and increasingly ailing, according to intelligence and medical reports. Stress, gum diseases and skin ailments are common.

The hostages have already passed Christmas and New Year inside the cramped building with the windows closed and no air conditioning despite the hot Lima summer. And they look likely to spend Easter there too.

"The basic problem is now almost the same as 90 days ago -- how to deal with the demand for freedom of MRTA prisoners. No political way to deal with this has yet been found," former captive and opposition legislator Javier Diez Canseco, released in the early days of the crisis, told Reuters.
"I think of the hostages every day, of what they are going through," he added.
The only activity at the siege site on Sunday was a Roman Catholic Mass given to the hostages by Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, and a low flyover by a police helicopter.

Cipriani, and two other members of a three-man guarantors commission overseeing negotiations between the government and rebels, were due to meet again on Monday with MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa and his second-in-command Rolly Rojas, local radio said.

The guarantors are meeting separately with the MRTA, and with government negotiator Domingo Palermo, in an effort to pave the way for a negotiated solution after 10 rounds of face-to-face talks apparently brought little more than a polite exchange of divergent positions.

Leading pollster Apoyo S.A. released a survey late Sunday showing that more than half of Peruvians believe the crisis will take at least one month more to resolve. Thirty-three percent of those surveyed believed the crisis would last a further one to three months, while another 20 percent thought it would take more than three months.

In better news for the government though, President Alberto Fujimori's personal approval rating was 52 percent in March, up from 46 percent the previous month, apparently on public backing for his tough handling of the crisis, Apoyo said.

While the MRTA rebels inside the residence kept a low profile over the weekend, their comrades outside kept up the propaganda war in e-mail and walkie-talkie communications with journalists covering the siege.

One senior MRTA leader identifying himself as "Comrade Alejandro", a member of the MRTA's high-command or policy-making body, told Reuters the army had launched an operation to flush guerrillas out of their jungle strongholds.
He said the army was deploying more than 500 soldiers to sweep through the central jungle provinces of Oxapampa and Chanchamayo in a bid to destroy the group's military bases.

The army denies there is any military operation. But local media has reported several MRTA captures over the last two weeks in the central jungle. And leading human rights group APRODEH alleged the whereabouts of four villagers in the area were still unknown after an army operation March 9 led to the detention of 21 peasants.
